University of Rhode Island Exam Proctoring Policy for Online Courses Online courses can and should use a wide variety of assessment methods, which should be designed to promote academic integrity.
In some disciplines proctored exams provide a useful tool for assessment of student learning in online courses.
When designing an online course, faculty should carefully balance the potential difficulties and costs for students who are unable to come to campus at a specific time for testing (i.e. working adults, students who live out of state, Faculty must provide clear guidance to students if they require a proctored exam.
The faculty member must state in their syllabus the beginning of the semester, if a proctored exam is required for the course.
They must note that the exam will be offered during one of the common exam times.
They must alert students as soon as possible: · The date, time, and place that the exam will be offered at the Kingston and/or Providence campuses.
The scheduled window period in which the exam is to be completed by those students who cannot come to campus and should include a link to the URI resources concerning proctored exams.

Scheduling Proctored Exams for Online Classes: ·Proctored final exams for online classes must be scheduled according to the appropriate policies of the campus where the course is offered (Kingston or Providence).
As soon as the exam is scheduled, faculty should make students aware of the time and date, and place It is the instructor's responsibility to ensure proper proctoring of the on campus exam.
Acceptable Exam Proctors outside of URI Students who cannot come to campus are responsible for making alternative arrangements for taking an exam by locating an acceptable proctor and location.
Proctors may not be friends or family members.
Acceptable proctors include: · Dean, academic department head, or official testing administrator of an accredited college or university Head librarian at a public library or a librarian with faculty status at an academic library ·Personnel at an exam testing center (such as ETS) Commanding officer at a military learning center Organizations that proctor have their own policies and exam takers need to be aware of these policies before taking the exam.

If there is a cost associated with an external proctored site, it is the responsibility of the student to pay that cost.
Approving a Proctor Form to the course instructor three weeks prior to the exam date.

University of Rhode Island Recommended Proctored Exam Procedure for Students If your instructor requires a proctored exam for your online course, it will be clearly noted in your syllabus on the first day of class.
You should carefully read your syllabus to understand the instructor's policy on arranging and completing a proctored exam.
Because online exams are offered in a "common exam space," the syllabus may not inclnde the exact day and time.
The instructor will provide that information to you at least four weeks before the exam is scheduled, sooner if possible.
As soon as possible, the instructor will inform you of: The date, time, and place that the exam will be offered, and which campus (Kingston or Providence).
OR if you are unable to come to campus: · The scheduled window period in which the exam is to be completed.
Finding an Exam Proctor if unable to come to URI campus Proctors may not be friends or family members.

Acceptable proctors include: · Dean, academic department head, or official testing administrator of an accredited college or university · Head librarian at an academic or public library ·Personnel at an exam testing center (such as ETS) · Commanding officer at a military learning center If there is a cost associated with an external proctored site, it is the responsibility of the student to pay that cost.
Getting a Proctor Approved After making arrangements with a proctor, the student must submit a Proctored Exam Request Form to the course instructor three weeks prior to the exam date.
Instructors will approve the arranged location and proctor, and confirm your contact with the proctor via email, telephone, or mail.
An instructor has the right not to approve a proctoring site, but will give you notice and a clear explanation so that you have the time and information to locate another proctor.
On the Day of the Exam You should meet your proctor at the agreed upon day, time and place.
You may bring with you any materials that the instructor has permitted or required for the exam (E.g.
Calculator, pencils, scratch paper, laptop). 1/10/2013 TAAC Report 2023-2024-01 Appendix A | Exam Proctoring Policy for Online Courses

Faculty Senate Executive Committee Report 2023-2024-03 - Proposed Creation of a Special Committee Faculty Senate - May 2, 2024 RATIONALE: According to Article II, Section 4 of Appendix B of the University Manual (Constitution of theFaculty Senate), the Senate shall establish such standing and special committees as it deems necessaryto carry out its functions.
During AY 2023-2024, the University community faced operational changes,including various administrative policy initiatives and the planned transition to a new budget model, thatstressed the ability of the Faculty Senate Executive Committee to respond appropriately and react in atimely fashion.
The FSEC has agreed that creating a special committee to advise the FSEC in these andrelated matters would improve the efficiency and effectiveness of the Faculty Senate.
This new groupcould assist in analyzing and making recommendations regarding any major operational changesemerging under the university strategic plan or under independent leadership of the President, VicePresidents, or Deans; including new budget models and their implementations; and any other specificoperational expenditures relevant to faculty.

Motion: to approve the creation of a Special Budget and Administration Committee to remain in effectuntil the end of Academic Year 2025-2026.
The Committee shall provide reports on their activities to theFaculty Senate at least annually and more often as directed by the FSEC or the Senate.
Any specificproposals for action will flow from the Special Committee to the FSEC and then to the Senate.
Activitiesof the Special Committee will include but not be limited to: review and if necessary develop measuresfor tracking major or incremental expenditures, with the aim of ensuring balanced support of facultyinterests; request information on the university’s performance toward any new goals set up under thenew incentive-based budget model (IBB) and raise questions about the correspondence of theseallocations against performance metrics (KPIs); monitor directions of administrative policies with the aimof supporting academic freedom and faculty efforts.

The new Special Committee shall makerecommendations to the executive committee and the senate about formal responses to: any plans orproposals by the committees and individuals tasked with the implementation and functioning of theincentive-based budget model; any positions or policy initiatives of the institutional research office,administrative policy groups, purchasing, capital projects, and similar groups as they may be identified orarise.
They may also engage in advocacy on behalf of the faculty for support of research, instruction,professional development, travel, course caps, and service time, so that faculty thrive in their workunder their contractual roles.
Membership will be three senators and 2 non senators, and the chair will be elected by the committeefollowing input from the senate executive committee.

Faculty Senate Executive Committee Report 2023-2024-04 - Proposed Creation of a Special Committee Faculty Senate - May 2, 2024 RATIONALE: According to Article II, Section 4 of Appendix B of the University Manual(Constitution of the Faculty Senate), the Senate shall establish such standing and specialcommittees as it deems necessary to carry out its functions.
The Executive Committee wasapproached by the Provost’s office regarding the need for more robust ongoing assessment andcontinuous improvement of the General Education Program.
They suggested the formation of a“steering committee” to recommend best practices for assessing the overall program and to helpdetermine if the current program is achieving the goals and outcomes envisioned in the enablinglegislation.
The FSEC and the General Education Committee (GEC) have worked on thisextensively this year and considered a variety of alternatives, including reconstituting theexisting standing committee and creating a new permanent joint committee.

FSEC ultimatelyagreed that creating a time-limited, special committee would be most effective at this stage.Other recommendations for future action can flow from this working group depending on theiranalysis and findings.
MOTION: to approve the creation of a Special Committee to serve in an advisory capacity to theGEC in the fulfillment of its duties related to the evaluation of the General Education Program:the Special Advisory Committee on General Education Program Evaluation.
GEC shall be responsible for designing specific tasks for the special committee to address overthe course of the 2024-2025 academic year and for making decisions relating to the membershipof the committee and securing commitments from faculty (and any other stakeholders deemedappropriate and advisable) to serve on the special committee by September 12, 2024 (Senateorientation meeting).
GEC shall report to the FS on the membership and planned tasks for the Special AdvisoryCommittee on General Education Program Evaluation at the September 19, 2024 meeting of theFaculty Senate.

GEC shall make recommendations to the FS regarding the advisability ofcontinuing the Special Advisory Committee on General Education Program Evaluation orconstituting a permanent committee at the April 2025 Faculty Senate meeting.

FACULTY SENATE OFFICE FACULTY SENATE LEGISLATION JANUARY 25, 2024 Faculty Senate Curriculum & Standards Committee Report 2023-2024-05B At the December 15, 2023 meeting of the Curriculum & Standards Committee, the following matters were considered and are now presented to the Faculty January 25, 2024 for approval.
SECTION I Curricular Matters Which Require Confirmation By The Faculty Senate NEW PROGRAMS COLLEGE OF ARTS & SCIENCES: Minor in Queer & Transgender Studies, see Appendix A The minor offers advance study of queer and transgender lives, cultures, and politics.
Students will complete 18 credits of coursework that includes the core requirement of GWS 210G.
The minor is an exploration of social justice issues through an interdisciplinary and intersectional framework.
Students will connect U.S. -centric issues to transnational networks, organizations, and other nation-states.
PROGRAM MODIFICATIONS COLLEGE OF ENGINEERING: BS Computer Engineering, see Appendix B Updating the professional elective requirements CSC courses.

COLLEGE OF THE ENVIRONMENT & LIFE SCIENCES: BS Environmental Science and Management, see Appendix C The faculty of the NRS department is proposing changes to the Environmental Science and Management major curriculum to in order to better serve the students enrolled in our major by giving them more choices.
There are three types of changes proposed: 1.
Reducing the number of categories in the concentration requirement from five to three (note that the number of credits required in the concentration will remain the same, 24 credits total.
The courses in the existing five categories (Biological or Ecologic al Sciences; Watersheds and Environmental Quality; Methods in Environmental Science; Natural Resources Management; Land use Management) will all be redistributed under CASC Report 2023-2024-05B Bill #23-24-16

the three new proposed categories (Environmental and Ecological Sciences, Methods and Applications, Environmental Management). 2.
Additional existing courses currently offered in other URI departments (i.e, BIO, GEO, WRT, please see attachments, courses highlighted in yellow) will be included as offerings in concentration requirements to provide students with more choices in the major.
No new courses are proposed or added.
Please see letters of support attached from BIO, GEO, and WRT.
In addition, the program description has been edited to reflect these proposed changes and revised for clarity and length.
COLLEGE OF HEALTH STUDIES: Specialization in Global & Environmental Health (BS Health Studies), see Appendix D We are requesting the addition of NRS 326 be added to the Global and Environmental specialization.
Support from NRS can be provided.
Specialization in Health & Aging Services (BS Human Development and Family Science), see Appendix E Aging and Health Services is a current concentration area within the HDF major .
Propose to change course requirement from HDF 431 to HDF 421.

BA Psychology, see Appendix F The BA degree in Psychology requires 120 total credits with a minimum of 32 credits (maximum 47) in Psychology.
At present, BA Psychology majors must complete 42 credits of courses listed at the 300 -level or higher prior to degree completion/graduation.
We are seeking to make a change in that policy by reducing the 42 credit hours to 30 credit hours at 300- level or higher.
We wish to do so for several reasons, but principally because we find that transfer and more mature students often end up extending their graduation date when enrolling in the added 300- level and higher courses, due to out-of-discipline pre-requisite requirements.
It is the sole change we are pursuing.
BS Public Health, see Appendix G We are requesting to change the major from health studies to public health.
We are also adding one core course (HLT 201) and reducing the number of free electives at the 300 or 400 level to 9 (from 12).
BS Kinesiology, see Appendix H Add KIN 464G and KIN 482 to the list of options for professional electives.
These have recently been added to our course offerings.

They are currently accepted as professional electives under the "or other health related class" descriptor, but listing them individually will make options more clear for students.
INTERDISCIPLINARY NEUROSCIENCE PROGRAM: BS Clinical Neuroscience, see Appendix I The changes proposed include new program language/description (very minor), as well as changes to some of the courses for the Clinical track.
This includes the addition of courses that are available to our students in other tracks (CHM 227, 226, 228, PHY 112, 186) and removal of some courses that are either no longer offered or not available to our students (i.e.
CMD 280G, PSY 205G, 261, 275, 384).
Please see the updated curriculum sheet.
